title: Psalm 59: Dogs at Evening, Praise in the Morning
summary: With killers watching his house, David asks God to deliver him from bloodthirsty men who prowl like dogs at night. He calls God his strength and fortress, asks that his enemies be humbled rather than simply killed so that God's rule will be known, and ends by singing of God's loving devotion in the morning.
story: Psalm 59 is the last of the three psalms set to “Do Not Destroy” (57 to 59), and in the order of David's story it comes earliest. Its heading takes us back to the first attempt on David's life at home, before his years in caves and foreign cities. Psalms 56 and 57 found him in Gath and a cave; this one finds him in his own house, with his wife Michal as his only ally. The psalm also widens its view beyond David's personal danger: it speaks repeatedly of the nations and asks that God's rule over Jacob be known to the ends of the earth. The next psalm, 60, will turn fully to national warfare.
historical:
The heading ties the psalm to 1 Samuel 19:11-17. Saul sent messengers to watch David's house and kill him in the morning. Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, warned him, let him down through a window, and put a household idol in his bed covered with clothes to buy time. The psalm's picture of enemies who come back at evening and prowl around the city, and of David singing in the morning (verse 16), fits that night of watching well.

The psalm also raises a question. It speaks of “all the nations” (verses 5 and 8) and asks God to show that he rules “over Jacob,” language more natural for a king facing foreign enemies than for a young man hiding from Saul. Some scholars think the psalm was composed later for a king or for the community under foreign threat, and the heading was added to connect it with David's story. Others think David, as the anointed future king, saw his enemies as enemies of God's people and used national language for them, or that the psalm was adapted for wider use after his time. The heading is present in the Hebrew and the ancient Greek translation, but, as elsewhere, its origin is debated.
cultural:
Dogs in the ancient Near East were rarely pets. Most towns had packs of half-wild dogs that scavenged at night for scraps and carcasses, growling and fighting over food, and they were widely regarded as unclean and dangerous (1 Kings 14:11; 21:23). To compare enemies to such dogs was a strong insult. The picture of verses 6, 14, and 15 is of men circling the house after dark, restless, hungry, and noisy.

The night-and-morning contrast reflects how people experienced time. Night was when danger was greatest, when thieves and attackers moved and there was little light. Morning was the time of rescue and of justice, when city courts sat at the gate and God's help was expected (Psalm 46:5; 30:5). David's move from watching through the night to singing in the morning follows the shape of that deliverance.
literary: The psalm is built with two refrains used twice each. The first, about the enemies returning in the evening, snarling like dogs, appears in verses 6 and 14. The second, a confession of God as strength and fortress, appears in verses 9 and 17, with small variations. The result is two parallel halves: verses 1 to 9 and verses 10 to 17, each moving from the threat to the refrain of trust. Within the halves, there is a sharp contrast between the dogs who return in the evening and David who sings in the morning, and between the enemies who ask “For who can hear us?” (verse 7) and the God who laughs at them (verse 8, echoing Psalm 2:4). Verse 11, “Do not kill them,” is a surprising request that the enemies be humbled slowly so their fall can be a lesson, followed by verse 13, which asks God to consume them. The tension between the two is part of the prayer's honesty.

outline.t: A plea for rescue from bloodthirsty men
Dogs prowling the city, and God's laughter
Refrain: God my strength and fortress
Humble them, so God's rule will be known
Morning song to God, my fortress and loving God

doctrines.note: The enemies think no one hears them, but God laughs at them and rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth. Human plots, however threatening at night, are small before God's rule.
David calls God “my God of loving devotion” in verses 10 and 17. God's covenant love is not only something he gives but part of how David names him.
David asks that the enemies be brought down in a way that teaches his people and the world. Judgment in this psalm has a public purpose: to make God's justice and rule known.

words.note: Misgav, fortress or high refuge. The word comes from a root meaning to be high, and it describes a stronghold set on a height, out of the enemy's reach. It appears three times (verses 9, 16, and 17). A man trapped in his own house calls God his high place of safety.

Kelev, dog. Twice the enemies are compared to dogs prowling the city (verses 6 and 14). In the ancient world dogs were scavengers, not companions, and the word could be a term of contempt (1 Samuel 17:43; 24:14).

Boqer, morning. In verse 16 David proclaims God's loving devotion in the morning. In the Psalms morning is often the moment of rescue and renewed praise after a night of danger or grief (Psalm 30:5; 46:5).

christ: David was hunted by men who watched and waited for a chance to kill him, and so was Jesus: the Gospels describe leaders who watched him closely and plotted to destroy him (Mark 3:2, 6). At the crucifixion Psalm 22:16 describes the sufferer surrounded by dogs, and the Gospel writers saw that psalm fulfilled at the cross. Psalm 59 shares that imagery, though the New Testament does not quote it directly. The rhythm of night followed by morning song finds its fullest expression in the resurrection, which the Gospels place early on the first day of the week (Mark 16:2). The request that God's rule be known to the ends of the earth is answered, in the Christian reading, when the risen Christ sends his followers to all nations (Matthew 28:18-20). These are thematic connections rather than direct prophecies.

hard.q: Why does David ask God not to kill his enemies (verse 11) and then ask God to consume them (verse 13)?
hard.a: The two requests can seem contradictory. One common reading is that David asks for a slow and visible judgment rather than a sudden one: if the enemies simply vanished, people would quickly forget, but if they were humbled and scattered, their fall would stand as a lasting lesson about God's rule. On this reading, consuming them in verse 13 refers to ending their power rather than killing them outright. Others see a real tension within the prayer, the kind of honest conflict that often appears in the Psalms when someone prays in danger, and think the psalm is not trying to resolve it logically. Both readings agree that the purpose of the judgment David asks for is that people will know God rules.

questions: The enemies say, “For who can hear us?” Why do people act as though no one sees or hears them? How does knowing that God hears change the way you act?
David moves from nighttime danger to morning praise. What has helped you move from fear to praise in a difficult time?
David wants his enemies' downfall to teach people about God. How can justice serve a purpose beyond punishment?
